title: Sects show who is approved
source_text: Εἰ δὲ ταῦτ᾿ ἔχει ἀκολουθίαν, πῶς οὐχὶ ὁμοίως ἀπολογησόμεθα καὶ περὶ τῶν ἐν Χριστιανοῖς αἱρέσεων; περὶ ὧν πάνυ θαυμασίως ὁ Παῦλος εἰρηκέναι μοι δοκεῖ τό· „δεῖ γὰρ καὶ αἱρέσεις ἐν ὑμῖν εἶναι, ἵνα οἱ δόκιμοι φανεροὶ γένωνται (ἐν ὑμῖν) .“ ὡς γὰρ δόκιμος ἐν ἰατρικῇ ὁ διὰ τὸ γυμνάσασθαι ἐν ποικίλαις αἱρέσεσι καὶ εὐγνωμόνως ἐξητακέναι τὰς πλείονας ἑλόμενος τὴν διαφέρουσαν, καὶ ὡς ὁ πάνυ προκόπτων ἐν φιλοσοφίᾳ ἀπὸ τοῦ πλείονα ἐγνωκέναι ἐγγυμνασάμενος αὐτοῖς καὶ τῷ κρατήσαντι προσθέμενος λόγῳ· οὕτως εἴποιμ᾿ ἂν καὶ τὸν ἐπιμελῶς ἐνιδόντα ταῖς ἰουδαϊσμοῦ καὶ χριστιανισμοῦ αἱρέσεσι σοφώτατον Χριστιανὸν γενέσθαι. ὁ δ᾿ ἐγκαλῶν τῷ λόγῳ διὰ τὰς αἱρέσεις ἐγκαλέσαι ἂν καὶ τῇ Σωκράτους διδασκαλίᾳ, ἀφ᾿ οὗ τῆς διατριβῆς πολλαὶ γεγόνασιν οὐ τὰ αὐτὰ φρονούντων σχολαί· ἀλλὰ καὶ Πλάτωνος ἐγκαλέσαι ἄν τις τοῖς δόγμασι δι᾿ Ἀριστοτέλην, ἀποφοιτήσαντα τῆς διατριβῆς αὐτοῦ ἐν καινοτομίαις· περὶ οὗ καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω εἰρήκαμεν. δοκεῖ δέ μοι ὁ Κέλσος ἐγνωκέναι τινὰς αἱρέσεις μηδὲ τοῦ ὀνόματος τοῦ Ἰησοῦ κοινωνούσας ἡμῖν. τάχα γὰρ περιήχητο περὶ τῶν καλουμένων Ὀφιανῶν καὶ τῶν Καϊανῶν, καὶ εἴ τις ἄλλη τοιαύτη ἐξ ὅλων ἀποφοιτήσασα τοῦ Ἰησοῦ συνέστη γνώμη· πλὴν οὐδὲν τοῦτο πρὸς τὸ ἐγκλητέον εἶναι τὸν Χριστιανῶν λόγον.
pass_a_gloss: If these have consistency (ἀκολουθία), how shall we not similarly make defence (ἀπολογησόμεθα) about the sects among Christians? About which Paul seems to me to have said most wonderfully: 'For there must (δεῖ) also be sects among you, that the approved (δόκιμοι) may become manifest (φανεροί) among you.' For as approved in medicine is the one who, through having trained (γυμνάσασθαι) in varied sects and having examined (ἐξητακέναι) fairly (εὐγνωμόνως) the most of them, chose (ἑλόμενος) the superior one (τὴν διαφέρουσαν); and as the one greatly advancing (προκόπτων) in philosophy [is he who], from having known more, has trained himself in them and attached himself (προσθέμενος) to the prevailing (κρατήσαντι) argument; so I would say also that one who has carefully looked into (ἐπιμελῶς ἐνιδόντα) the sects of Judaism and Christianity becomes a most wise (σοφώτατον) Christian. But one accusing (ἐγκαλῶν) the word because of the sects would accuse also the teaching of Socrates, from whose school (διατριβή) many schools (σχολαί) of those not thinking the same have arisen; and one might accuse Plato's doctrines (δόγματα) because of Aristotle, who departed (ἀποφοιτήσαντα) from his school in innovations (καινοτομίαι); about whom we spoke above too. Celsus seems to me to have known some sects not even sharing the name of Jesus with us. For perhaps he had heard the noise about (περιήχητο) the so-called Ophites (Ὀφιανοί) and Cainites (Καϊανοί), and any other such opinion (γνώμη) that arose having departed wholly (ἐξ ὅλων) from Jesus; but this is nothing toward the Christians' doctrine (λόγος) being accusable (ἐγκλητέον).
pass_b_english: If this reasoning holds, why should we not make the same defence for the sects among Christians as well? Of these, Paul seems to me to have spoken most admirably: “For there must also be sects among you, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Corinthians 11:19). For the man approved in medicine is the one who, having trained himself in various sects and fairly examined most of them, has chosen the best; and the man who makes great progress in philosophy is the one who, having come to know more of them, has trained himself in them and attached himself to the argument that prevailed. In the same way I would say that one who has looked carefully into the sects of Judaism and of Christianity becomes a most wise Christian.

But anyone who accuses the word because of the sects would also accuse the teaching of Socrates, from whose school there have come many schools of men who do not think alike. One might also accuse Plato’s doctrines because of Aristotle, who broke away from his school by introducing new ideas; we have spoken of him earlier too.

Celsus, it seems to me, knew of some sects that do not even share the name of Jesus with us. Perhaps he had heard talk of the so-called Ophites and Cainites, and of any other such school of thought that has arisen by breaking away from Jesus entirely. But this does nothing to show that the teaching of Christians is open to accusation.

choices.choice: 1 Corinthians 11:19 quoted with 'ἐν ὑμῖν' at the end as an editorial supplement in the staging text (accepted; it stands in the New Testament text). αἱρέσεις kept as 'sects' (see 3.12); modern Bibles often have 'factions' here. The second comparison clause (philosophy) is elliptical in the Greek; 'is the one who' is supplied from the parallel clause. 'τὴν διαφέρουσαν' = 'the one that excels', rendered 'the best'. 'ἀποφοιτήσασα' (of the sects) is the same verb used of Aristotle leaving Plato's school, so both are rendered 'broke away' / 'breaking away'. 'γνώμη' rendered 'school of thought'. 'ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω' points to Origen's earlier comparison of Aristotle leaving Plato (Against Celsus 2.12). Ophites and Cainites are named Gnostic groups; Origen treats the Ophites at length later (6.24-38).
'If these things follow, how shall we not' changed to 'If this reasoning holds, why should we not' (ἀκολουθία; less stiff).
'from knowing more of them' changed to 'having come to know more of them' (ἀπὸ τοῦ πλείονα ἐγνωκέναι).

'any other such opinion that has arisen and has departed wholly from Jesus' changed to 'any other such school of thought that has arisen by breaking away from Jesus entirely' (keeps the ἀποφοιτάω echo of Aristotle).
'deserves to be accused' changed to 'is open to accusation' (ἐγκλητέον).
